title: Ukrainians in Italy
summary: Ukrainians in Italy primarily consist of recent labor migrants, with a significant presence in the caregiving sector. As of 2020, there were 223,000 Ukrainians in Italy, making them the fourth-largest immigrant group in the country.

sections.heading: Migration and Employment
paragraphs: Ukrainians in Italy are largely recent labor migrants. As of 2020, the population of [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]] with valid permits in Italy was 223,000. A considerable number of [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] women work as caretakers for the elderly, terminally ill, children, or entire families. Due to a lack of in-home caregivers among native Italians, who often view this profession as physically demanding and emotionally taxing, Ukrainians have been welcomed as a solution to this shortage.

sections.heading: Historical Context
paragraphs: The historical ties between [[ukraine|Ukraine]] and Italy date back to the 15th century, exemplified by scholar Yuriy [[drohobych|Drohobych]] from present-day [[western-ukraine|Western Ukraine]], who served as the rector of Bologna University. Notable Ukrainian figures such as [[hryhorii-skovoroda|Hryhoriy Skovoroda]] and [[lesya-ukrainka|Lesya Ukrainka]] visited Italy during the 18th and 19th centuries. Following the Union of Brest, Rome became a significant center for the [[ukrainian-greek-catholic-church|Ukrainian Catholic Church]]. During World War I, many Ukrainian prisoners of war were detained in Italy, and in the aftermath, the [[ukrainian-peoples-republic|Ukrainian People's Republic]] established a diplomatic mission in Italy from 1919 to 1920, led by Dmytro Antonovych, along with a separate mission for the [[west-ukrainian-peoples-republic|West Ukrainian People's Republic]]. The Interwar period saw prominent Ukrainian political and cultural figures reside in Italy, including [[yevhen-konovalets|Yevhen Konovalets]], and a Ukrainian community was founded in Rome in 1933. After World War II, approximately 15,000 Ukrainians, including soldiers from the Ukrainian National Army, were present in Italy.

sections.heading: Demographics
paragraphs: According to a report by the National Institute of Statistics (Istat), there were 223,782 Ukrainians in Italy as of 2012, with around 80% being women. However, estimates of the total Ukrainian population in Italy, including those working or residing illegally, range from 600,000 to 1 million. While many Ukrainian immigrants express a desire to return to Ukraine, some are opting to remain in Italy permanently. Following the Russian [[full-scale-russo-ukrainian-war|invasion of Ukraine]], 112,098 refugees arrived in Italy by May 2022, comprising 58,334 women, 15,256 men, and 38,508 minors.

sections.heading: Religion
paragraphs: A survey conducted by ISTAT in 2011 and 2012 revealed the religious affiliations of Ukrainians in Italy. Approximately 90.8% identified as Christians, with 68% being Orthodox Christians, 22.5% Catholics, and 0.3% Protestants. Additionally, 0.1% identified as Muslims, 5.6% as non-religious, and 3.5% adhered to other religions.

sections.heading: Cultural Contributions
paragraphs: Among the cultural contributions of Ukrainians in Italy is the amateur theatre group 'Berehynia,' which reflects the community's artistic engagement and cultural heritage.
